Who Bridges Safety? Identifying and Targeting Cross-Lingual Shared Safety Pathways

Tracing cross-layer safety pathways reveals a shared target for transferring refusal behavior across languages.

Miao Shuyi

August 10, 2026 ·Preprint ·3-minute read ·Read the paper ·PDF ·Code
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

Who Bridges Safety studies multilingual safety as a problem of signal propagation. It identifies cross-layer pathways using both co-activation and activation-propagation measurements, then examines the paths shared by high-resource and non-high-resource languages. The unit of analysis is a connection between components, extending the view provided by isolated-neuron measurements.

The resulting shared pathways guide selective alignment. Masking experiments test their functional relevance, while targeted updates examine whether strengthening the shared computation improves refusal behavior in less well-protected languages without broadly changing the model.

Cross-layerUnit of mechanistic analysis
Shared pathsSelective alignment target
Held-outLanguage-transfer evaluation

A shared safety component matters through the computation it helps carry across layers and languages.

Why this matters

Models can understand a language while failing to apply a safety judgment in it. Locating individual safety-related neurons helps identify relevant components, but leaves open how their signals combine and propagate into a refusal decision.

How it works

  1. Identify language-specific safety pathways from cross-layer co-activation and activation propagation.
  2. Intersect the pathway sets across languages and compare targeted masking with size-matched random controls.
  3. Concentrate alignment updates on shared pathway parameters and evaluate multilingual safety together with general capabilities.

What the study finds

The selected masking controls show larger safety degradation when shared pathways are disrupted than when matched random pathways are disrupted. Multilingual evaluations compare targeted alignment with preference-optimization and cross-language baselines; additional experiments examine training efficiency, general capability retention, and leave-one-language-out transfer.

What this means

The work makes the connectivity of a safety mechanism an explicit research target. A model may contain relevant components yet fail to coordinate them effectively in a particular language. Path-level analysis connects those two possibilities to interventions that can be tested.

This suggests a mechanism-aware approach to transfer: identify a shared computation, validate its role, and then optimize where that computation is carried. The evidence supports the studied pathway constructions and languages; how broadly those bridges generalize remains a question for further controlled evaluation.
